explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, listening is the pick. The Teacher says to draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools (Ecclesiastes 5:1). Those fools, he says, do not know that they do wrong. So he points us toward listening, and away from the sacrifice of fools.

Singing sounds nice, and I would happily hum along. But that's not the word in this verse. The Teacher says to draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools (Ecclesiastes 5:1). The word he gives is listen.

Giving feels like the safe guess, friend, because a sacrifice is something you give. But the Teacher says to draw near to listen rather than to offer the sacrifice of fools (Ecclesiastes 5:1). Listening is what he puts first. The fools in that verse are the ones who offer without knowing they do wrong.

True, friend. The Teacher says, "For God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few." (Ecclesiastes 5:2). That "for" ties the two together. God is in heaven, we are on earth, and so our words are few.

It's actually true, friend. Look at Ecclesiastes 5:2, where the Teacher says, "For God is in heaven and you are on earth. So let your words be few." That's his reason, right there in the verse. God is in heaven, we are on earth, and so our words are few.

That's the one. The Teacher says, "As a dream comes through many cares, so the speech of a fool comes with many words." (Ecclesiastes 5:3). A fool's speech and a pile of words go together. A few good words beat a whole bakery full of noise.

Good guess, since the Teacher is a king himself (Ecclesiastes 1:1). But the verse doesn't point at kings at all. It says, "…so the speech of a fool comes with many words." (Ecclesiastes 5:3). Many words belong to the fool in this picture.

I see why a priest comes to mind, with the house of God right there in verse 1. But the Teacher never mentions a priest in this picture. He says, "…so the speech of a fool comes with many words." (Ecclesiastes 5:3). The one with all the words is the fool.
Not quite, friend. The Teacher says the opposite: "When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it…" (Ecclesiastes 5:4). No taking your time. He ends the verse with "Fulfill your vow."

False is right, friend. The Teacher says, "When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow." (Ecclesiastes 5:4). No delay. I'd say that's one deadline I can't hit the snooze button on.

explanations.answer: Not making a vow at all
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The Teacher says, "It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it." (Ecclesiastes 5:5). An empty promise is worse than staying quiet. Think before you promise, then keep what you promised.

A smaller vow sounds like a clever workaround, friend. But the Teacher never offers one. He says, "It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it." (Ecclesiastes 5:5). The better thing is not vowing at all.

explanations.answer: Letting a priest vow for you
explanations.explanation: Handing the vow off to somebody else would be a neat trick, friend. But nobody in this passage does that. The Teacher says, "It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it." (Ecclesiastes 5:5). Better than a broken vow is no vow at all.

A gift would be a sweet thing to call a vow, but that's not the word. The Teacher says, "…do not tell the messenger that your vow was a mistake." (Ecclesiastes 5:6). The word he uses is mistake.
A secret makes a good plot twist, friend, but it's not in this verse. The Teacher says, "…do not tell the messenger that your vow was a mistake." (Ecclesiastes 5:6). The word is mistake.

Careful, friend, this one is true. Look at the end of Ecclesiastes 5:6, where the Teacher asks, "Why should God be angry with your words and destroy the work of your hands?" He asks it right after saying not to tell the messenger that your vow was a mistake. I'd call that a question worth sitting with.
That's the finish, baker. After all the warnings about words and vows, the Teacher says, "Therefore, fear God." (Ecclesiastes 5:7). Just three words, and I think they hit harder for it.

I see the pull of that one, friend, but the Teacher goes the other way. He has just warned us not to be hasty in our hearts before God (Ecclesiastes 5:2). His closing words are "Therefore, fear God." (Ecclesiastes 5:7).

Bold sounds exciting, friend, but that's not what the Teacher says here. He says, "Do not be quick to speak…" and "…let your words be few." (Ecclesiastes 5:2). He wraps it up with "Therefore, fear God." (Ecclesiastes 5:7).
